model.label: Compulsory social health insurance (General Health Insurance) with a single public payer, the Social Security Institution, funded by payroll contributions and general taxes; most care delivered by Ministry of Health facilities, with private hospitals under contract

overview.statement: Between 2003 and 2013 the Health Transformation Programme reorganized how the Turkish health system was financed, delivered and regulated.

Under that programme, the General Health Insurance Scheme set up in 2006 combined five existing insurance schemes into compulsory social health insurance with a single payer, the Social Security Institution (SSI).

Since 2019, after Türkiye moved from a parliamentary to a presidential system, health policy has been set by the Health and Food Policies Council under the President, with the Ministry of Health and its provincial directorates carrying it out (workforce planning, regulation of medicines and devices, research).
Public providers dominate service delivery; private providers either work under contract with the SSI or are paid directly by patients.

Since a family practitioner scheme began in 2011, family physicians and family health centres have been the main providers of preventive and curative primary care, each serving a population list set by Ministry of Health population and distance criteria; patients may change family practitioner once every three months.

At the end of 2024 Türkiye had 1,544 hospitals in active service: 940 run by the Ministry of Health, 69 by universities and 535 private, with 270,212 beds in total (172,406 in Ministry of Health hospitals).

financing.statement: For workers covered by the full social insurance package, the General Health Insurance contribution is 12.5% of earnings subject to contributions: 5 percentage points paid by the employee and 7.5 by the employer.

People insured only for health (and some other listed groups) pay 12% of their contribution base, while those enrolled under the residual category of Article 60(1)(g) pay 3%, a rate the President may raise to as much as 12%.

Contributions are charged on earnings between a floor and a ceiling: the daily floor is one-thirtieth of the age-appropriate minimum wage and the ceiling is 9 times the daily floor for insured people over 16.

Since 2010 public sources have paid for around 78% of current health spending; in 2019 public spending on health equalled 3.4% of GDP, similar to other upper middle-income countries but below the EU (6.0%) and WHO European Region (5.0%) averages.
In TURKSTAT's health accounts, public current health expenditure was 3.7% of GDP in 2024 (1,630 billion lira out of a GDP of 44,587 billion lira).

financing.statement: Out-of-pocket payments fell from 28.9% of current health spending in 2000 to 16.9% in 2019, below the 2019 averages of the EU (20.9%) and the WHO European Region (28.7%).
TURKSTAT figures show out-of-pocket payments at 18.8% of total health expenditure and 20.2% of current health expenditure in 2024, up from 15.9% and 17.0% in 2021.

locator.figure: Figures 11.17 and 11.18, out-of-pocket share of total and of current health expenditure by years

financing.statement: Tax relief for private cover: employees can deduct health and other personal insurance premiums they pay to insurers based in Türkiye from their wages for income tax, up to 15% of the month's wage and no more than the annual minimum wage in total.

covered.statement: In 2019, 98.8% of the population had social health insurance, up from 71.6% in 2003 and 93.2% in 2008.

Most long-term residents are eligible for social health insurance, and some groups are covered free with no eligibility conditions: children, and people needing long-term medical support, infectious disease care, drug addiction services, childbirth care or emergency care.
The state must ensure coverage for people receiving social benefits and for people whose monthly income per person is below one third of the gross minimum wage.
Citizens who fall outside every other category of the law and have no right to health insurance in another country are counted as General Health Insurance members.

Since 2007 the SSI has decided each year, through the Health Implementation Guide, which services are publicly covered; the package pays for almost all preventive, inpatient and outpatient care except cosmetic surgery, with some limits on assisted reproduction and dental treatment.
Registered refugees have coverage similar to the general population, but unregistered refugees and migrants and those with precarious legal status lack full coverage.

Apart from exempt cases (people under 18, people medically dependent on others' care, traffic accidents, emergencies, work accidents and occupational disease, notifiable infectious diseases, addiction treatment and some others), members generally need 30 days of General Health Insurance contributions in the year before they seek care.

Members in the categories of Article 60(1)(a)(2) and 60(1)(g) must, in addition, have no contribution or related debt older than 60 days when they seek care, unless the debt is being paid under a deferral and instalment arrangement.

cost_sharing.statement: Patients pay 20% coinsurance on prescriptions and medical devices (10% for retirees) and a fixed co-payment for outpatient visits; primary care visits are exempt, to encourage people to start there rather than go straight to secondary or tertiary care.

The law sets the outpatient doctor or dentist visit co-payment at a base of 20 lira and the co-payment for outpatient medicines and external prostheses at 10% to 20%, with the SSI choosing the rate according to criteria such as avoiding unnecessary use, how vital the service is and the person's income.

The SSI may waive or lower the visit co-payment at primary care, raise it up to tenfold at secondary and tertiary providers depending on the level of care, whether the provider is public or private and whether the patient was referred, and halve it for patients referred from primary care.
The SSI may also charge a prescription co-payment of 3 lira for up to three items or boxes of medicine, including prescriptions written by family physicians, and 1 lira for each further item.
Since a January 2025 amendment, the 1, 20 and 3 lira amounts rise every year by the revaluation rate set under the Tax Procedure Law.

Caps apply: the co-payment for external prostheses and orthoses may not exceed 75% of the minimum wage, and the inpatient co-payment may not exceed a quarter of the minimum wage per stay or one minimum wage in a calendar year.

Contracted providers other than public ones (including foundation universities) may charge patients an additional fee on top of the SSI tariff; the President sets a ceiling of up to twice the tariff and the SSI sets the rates within it.
Out-of-pocket spending is driven by fairly high co-payments for medicines and for outpatient services used without a referral.

financial_hardship.statement: Using TURKSTAT Household Budget Survey data and defining catastrophic spending as out-of-pocket health costs above 10% of household spending, Sulku and Kaya found the share facing it rose slightly from 4.28% in 2019 to 4.37% in 2022, while those above the threshold spent 21.88% of their budget on health in 2022, up from 19.53%.

In the same study, having insurance cut the risk of catastrophic spending by about 13%, but households with young children, older or disabled members faced higher risk, and the authors judged protection insufficient for disadvantaged groups.

A study of Household Budget Survey data for 2014-2023 found that although richer groups spent more in absolute terms, the burden relative to income fell disproportionately on lower-income households, and high out-of-pocket-to-income burdens became more concentrated after 2018.

additional_care.statement: In 2019, 9% of people had voluntary private health insurance, mainly to pay for care in private hospitals without an SSI contract or with a limited one, or as complementary cover for services outside the basic package.
Specialist outpatient care is provided in hospital outpatient departments, private doctors' offices and private outpatient centres.
At the end of 2024 the private sector also ran 551 specialty medical centres and 303 private outpatient clinics.

access.statement: Primary care has no gatekeeping role, so patients tend to go straight to more specialized facilities and overuse hospital services, particularly admissions and in-hospital tests.
Self-reported unmet need for medical examination because of cost, distance or waiting fell from 16.4% of the population in 2010 (EU 3.5%) to 1.9% in 2020, similar to the EU average.

access.statement: Unmet need varied sharply with income: in 2019 it reached 9% in the poorest fifth of the population against 0.4% in the richest.

access.statement: Despite bonus pay and compulsory service in deprived areas, health workers remain unevenly spread, leaving access unequal across regions, especially in the east and in rural areas.

access.statement: Hospital appointments are booked through the Central Physician Appointment System (MHRS) by phone, internet or mobile app; studies credit it with shorter hospital queues and high user satisfaction.

In a 2022 survey across 20 provinces, Syrian and Turkish respondents had similar predicted probabilities of a doctor visit in the past year (79.8% and 80.8%), though Syrians were less likely to use emergency departments (25.4% vs 31.75%).

outcomes.statement: The Global Burden of Disease study put Türkiye's Healthcare Access and Quality (HAQ) Index at 64.8 (95% uncertainty interval 62.1-67.7) for ages 0-74 in 2019, with 68.9 for ages 0-14, 71.3 for ages 15-64 and 61.5 for ages 65-74, an overall rise of 27.9 points since 1990.

outcomes.statement: Infant mortality was 8.9 per 1,000 live births in 2024, against 3.8 in the OECD and 3.1 in the EU (2023 data for the comparators).

outcomes.statement: Maternal mortality was 11.5 per 100,000 live births in 2024, close to the WHO European Region (11) and high-income country (10) figures for 2023.

locator.figure: Figure 2.12, international comparison of maternal mortality ratio

outcomes.statement: Noncommunicable diseases caused an estimated 89% of deaths in 2020; cancer was the leading cause of death in 2019 (112 deaths per 100,000), followed by ischaemic heart disease, respiratory disease, stroke and diabetes.

locator.section: 4 Improving the health of the population

outcomes.statement: Adult smoking barely fell, from 32.9% in 2000 to 30.7% in 2020, and 42.1% of men smoked in 2020, well above the male rates in the WHO European Region (32%) and EU (27.5%).

locator.section: 4 Improving the health of the population

outcomes.statement: Tuberculosis incidence fell from 28.1 to 13.6 per 100,000 people by 2019, staying below the WHO European Region average (20.5 in 2019).

locator.section: 3 Generating resources, providing services and ensuring access

outcomes.statement: New HIV diagnoses rose from 0.7 per 100,000 people in 2009 to 3.9 in 2019, although incidence stayed below the regional average.

locator.section: 3 Generating resources, providing services and ensuring access

costs.statement: Current health expenditure was 4.9% of GDP in 2024, up from 3.6% in 2022 and 4.2% in 2023 (TURKSTAT health accounts).

costs.statement: In 2019 current health spending was 4.7% of GDP, down from 6% in 2009 and below the WHO European Region (7.6%) and EU (8.2%) averages.

Health spending per person roughly tripled from about US$ 400 PPP in 2000 to US$ 1,200 PPP in 2019, mainly because public spending rose from about US$ 250 to 925 PPP per person, most of it in the first ten years.

Public health spending as a share of GDP fell faster from 2009 to 2019 than in other countries; because GDP per person grew over the period, this meant a relative decline in public funds allocated to health.

Fourteen hospitals built and run under public-private partnerships scored higher on efficiency (data envelopment analysis, 2015-2023) after the switch than before, but the authors say long-term cost-benefit studies are needed before firm conclusions on the model.

Critics argue that the city hospitals built through public-private partnerships commit the state to long-term rental payments, reduce budget flexibility and raise financial risk; the government presents them as a way to modernize infrastructure quickly.

locator.section: Political economy of health reforms in Türkiye

costs.statement: Hospitals took more than half (53%) of Türkiye's health spending in 2021, the highest share among OECD members, against an OECD average of 39%.

what_works.statement: The Health Transformation Programme substantially expanded public health insurance, especially for the poorest groups, which improved access to care and financial protection.
Childhood vaccination is nearly universal: in 2019, 99% coverage for DTP3 and 97% for the first measles dose, above EU and WHO European Region averages.

locator.section: 3 Generating resources, providing services and ensuring access

what_works.statement: Infant mortality fell from 31.4 per 1,000 live births in 2009 to 8.6 in 2019, still above the EU average of 3.4; the review names the HTP's expanded maternal care and free coverage for children as a possible explanation.

locator.section: 4 Improving the health of the population

what_works.statement: Early evaluations rated the COVID-19 response positively, crediting earlier reforms, stronger primary care and public health, comprehensive electronic medical records and long experience with emergencies and disaster management.

locator.section: 4 Improving the health of the population

what_works.statement: Creating the SSI in 2006 brought fragmented social security schemes under one institution, pooling funds and giving people more equal access to services.

locator.section: Political economy of health reforms in Türkiye

what_works.statement: Registered Syrians living in their province of registration reported being satisfied with their access to health care.

problems.statement: Half of the households with catastrophic health spending in 2018 were already poor and at risk of becoming poorer still.
Türkiye has one of the highest rates of antibiotic use in the WHO European Region, and antimicrobial resistance is higher than in western and northern Europe.

Applications by physicians for the good-standing certificates needed to work abroad rose from 59 in 2012 to 2,685 in 2022, while recorded inflows of Turkish physicians to OECD countries rose from 77 to 645.

In a survey of 1,331 physicians, violence against health workers (81.6%), low pay (74.3%) and hard working conditions (59.8%) were the main reasons given for emigrating, and only 2 of 32 emigrated physicians interviewed were considering returning.

Specialists interviewed in one province (12 physicians) said the pay-for-performance scheme encourages patient-poaching and defensive decisions, appointment quotas make proper informed consent hard, and the rule that cuts off people with premium debt puts physicians in an unjust position.

Researchers point to out-of-pocket payments, high costs at contracted private hospitals and growing take-up of complementary insurance as signs that financial protection remains incomplete despite near-universal insurance.

Hospital registration staff interviewed in two public hospitals said equal formal access to the appointment system does not mean equal chances of getting care, because digital skills, social support, transport and time differ between patients.
Syrians who face registration obstacles experience severe barriers and fall back on expensive private care or informal Syrian clinics.
Air pollution is a major health risk; Türkiye had among the highest rates of premature death from air pollution in Europe in 2015.

locator.section: 4 Improving the health of the population

reforms.statement: January 2025: Law No. 7538 raised the statutory base of the outpatient visit co-payment from 2 to 20 lira and allowed the SSI to halve the co-payment for patients referred from primary care.
2024: the Ministry of Health counted 25 city hospitals with 37,132 beds.

locator.table: Table 7.1, number of hospitals and beds by branches, 2024

reforms.statement: Türkiye used the build-operate-transfer form of public-private partnership for its new city hospitals: 18 were planned, the first began operating in 2017 and the number reached 18 by the end of 2024.

Concern about the relatively high cost of PPP hospital projects has led the government to rely more on the general budget: six city hospitals were built that way in the past five years, 11 more are under construction with public funds and nine are in tendering or project development.
2020: the COVID-19 pandemic was used to recruit 44,000 health personnel; the review says it was too early to judge whether this growth would last.

locator.section: 3 Generating resources, providing services and ensuring access

reforms.statement: 2011-2017: a Public Hospital Unions model meant to run hospitals on business lines was introduced in 2011 and abolished in 2017 because of its bureaucratic and administrative burden.
